subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: researching housing and neighbourhood safety [Action]
passage: Sit, Trisha, before your father pays anyone a rupee. Your Shalini Bua has a story about that. When I was seventeen and heading to college in Nagpur, Papa and I lined up one hostel and two paying-guest rooms. We read what earlier residents had written, but I also phoned three seniors and asked plain things: how long is the commute, is the food edible, is it safe to walk back after evening class? Then Papa took a day off from his shop and we saw all three in person before anyone handed over a deposit. The cheapest room had a dark stairwell and a gate that locked at eight. I picked the hostel near the bus stop. It cost a little more, but I slept easily there for three years.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cheapest room?
qa.a: It had a dark stairwell and a gate that locked at eight.

qa.q: Why did Shalini phone seniors and ask such plain questions?
qa.a: She was cautious and wanted honest answers about the commute, the food and safety before any money changed hands.

qa.q: What could someone do if they cannot visit the places in person?
qa.a: They could take a video tour with a parent and talk to current residents, since that lets them see the place and hear honest experiences before paying.

qa.q: How might Papa have seen the extra visits?
qa.a: Papa may have found them tiring, but Papa probably felt reassured to see the places in person, since Shalini's safety and the deposit were both at stake.

grounding: With a parent, a student compares hostel and paying-guest options, asks seniors about commute, food and safety, and visits before paying any deposit.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: researching housing and neighbourhood safety [Action]
passage:
Uma had nine days before classes began in Bengaluru and one weekend when both parents could travel with her. The coaching institute's hostel had a waiting list, and the paying-guest places nearby all promised “safe, homely food, walking distance”.
So on the train they made a table: hostel or PG, rent, meals, curfew, distance, what reviews said. Two PGs had reviews mentioning broken locks, so they crossed those off. Then Uma called Hrithik, a senior from her school who had studied there last year.
“Ask about the walk at night,” he said. “The lane behind Green Villa has no lights. And the food at Sai PG is fine; the other one skipped dinner twice a week.”
On Saturday, in heavy rain, they visited three places. At Sai PG, Uma checked the lock on the door and the lights on the lane, and asked two girls on the stairs what the warden was like. Only after that did Appa pay the deposit.

qa.q: What did Hrithik say about the lane behind Green Villa?
How might Uma have felt visiting places in heavy rain with so little time?
qa.a: Uma was probably anxious about the short deadline but determined to see the places herself before any deposit was paid.

qa.q: What else could Uma's family check before deciding?
qa.a: Talk to the warden directly about rules and emergencies, and walk the route to the institute at the hour Uma would use it.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see being called for advice?
qa.a: Hrithik probably feels useful and trusted, glad to pass on details a review wouldn't show.

grounding: Shows a student with her parents comparing hostel and PG options, reading reviews, asking a senior about commute, food and safety, and visiting before paying a deposit.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: researching housing and neighbourhood safety [Action]
passage:
In the crowded lanes near the coaching centres of Mukherjee Nagar in Delhi, Omkar and his father spent Sunday doing what they had planned on paper. The list in Omkar's notebook had four places: the institute hostel and three paying-guest houses, with columns for rent, food, distance and “what seniors say”.
The night before, Omkar had messaged Zubin, a senior from their town, now in his second year. Zubin was blunt. “The cheap PG near the market floods every August. The hostel food is boring but regular. Check whether the PG gate closes at night.”
So they checked. At the first PG the owner said “all safe, no problem”, but the fire exit was padlocked. They left. At the second, the commute was forty minutes by bus, not the “ten minutes” in the advert. At the hostel, Omkar tasted the dal, saw the warden's desk by the gate, and walked the route to class himself.
They paid the hostel deposit only on the way out.

qa.q: What was wrong at the first PG?
What might Omkar have felt when the advert's ten minutes turned out to be forty?
qa.a: Omkar probably felt annoyed and more cautious, seeing that adverts couldn't be trusted without checking.

qa.q: What else could Omkar ask before moving in?
qa.a: Ask current residents how the warden handles problems at night, since that matters more than the brochure.

qa.q: How might Omkar's father see the day?
qa.a: His father likely feels relieved that checking in person ruled out an unsafe place, and confident about the hostel.

grounding: Shows a student with a parent comparing hostel and PG options, using a senior's advice on commute, food and safety, and visiting before paying any deposit.
